questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the discrete/continuous split in Tableau, per Lesson 5.
options: A discrete field creates headers when placed on a shelf; a continuous field creates an axis
Discrete pills are colored green, and continuous pills are colored blue
A date field can be set to either discrete or continuous, and the two settings produce genuinely different views of the same field
Discrete/continuous is identical to the Dimension/Measure split — every Dimension is discrete and every Measure is continuous, with no exceptions
Converting a field between discrete and continuous is independent of converting it between Dimension and Measure
questions.explain: Discrete fields produce headers, continuous fields produce axes — that's the behavior the color-coding (blue for discrete, green for continuous) signals, the reverse of option B. A date field can genuinely be set either way, producing headers like 'Q1, Q2, Q3' or a true timeline axis. And discrete/continuous is a completely separate switch from Dimension/Measure — you could, in principle, have a discrete Measure or continuous Dimension, even though most fields stay close to their sensible default.

questions.prompt: A student argues that Postal Code must belong in the Measures section of the Data pane, since its values are numbers. Per Lesson 5, why is that reasoning wrong?
options: Tableau's data-type-based guess is only a default — a numeric field like Postal Code is really a Dimension, since you'd never meaningfully sum or average it
Tableau never allows a numeric field to become a Measure under any circumstances
Postal Code is automatically continuous, and continuous fields can never be classified as Measures
Only text fields are ever allowed to be Dimensions in Tableau
questions.explain: Tableau makes a reasonable default guess from data type — numbers usually become Measures — but it's only a default. A field like Postal Code is numeric but behaves like a Dimension: it describes/categorizes rather than measures something, so dragging it to the Dimensions section (or converting it) is the right call, exactly the example the lesson gives.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: per Lesson 3, one row in Sample Superstore represents a single ________ on an order — one product, on one order, shipped to one customer.
questions.explain: Sample Superstore's granularity is one row per order line item — one product on one order shipped to one customer — not one row per order or per customer. Knowing this granularity up front is exactly why the course keeps returning to this same dataset instead of re-explaining structure every lesson.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of Lesson 6's first-visualization exercise in the correct order.
items: Drag Order Date onto Columns and set it to show Year
Drag Profit onto Rows, then drag Sales onto Rows next to it
Drag Region onto Color on the Marks card
Select both rows and choose the stacked bar chart option in the Show Me panel
questions.explain: The exercise builds the view's shape first — Order Date (Year) on Columns, then both Profit and Sales stacked on Rows — adds Region to Color for the eventual legend, and only then uses Show Me's multi-select-and-pick step to convert the whole thing into stacked bars. Show Me rearranges shelves you've already populated; it doesn't work from an empty view.

questions.prompt: A teammate opens a workbook and Tableau shows the 'Extract Not Found' dialog because the underlying .hyper file was deleted. They want Tableau to rebuild the extract completely from the original data source, as if creating it fresh. Which of Tableau's four recovery options does that?
options: Regenerate the extract
Locate the extract
Remove the extract
Deactivate the extract
questions.explain: Regenerate the extract re-creates it entirely from the original source, exactly as if building it for the first time. Locate only points Tableau to a relocated file (which doesn't exist here, since it was deleted); Remove deletes the reference and falls back to a Live connection; Deactivate just stops using the reference for now without rebuilding anything.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about Live connections and Extracts, per Lesson 9.
options: An Extract is required when publishing to Tableau Public, since it doesn't allow live database connections
A Live connection stores a local snapshot of the data in Tableau's Hyper engine
Extract performance is often dramatically faster than Live because Hyper is built specifically for analytical queries
A Live connection can be used entirely offline, since it never depends on reaching the original source
Heavy interactive use of a Live connection repeatedly puts load on the original source system
questions.explain: Tableau Public requires Extract since it can't hold live database connections. Extracts are typically faster because Hyper is purpose-built for analytical queries. And because Live sends a fresh query to the source on every interaction, heavy interactive use repeatedly loads that source system — the opposite of option D, since Live specifically requires reaching the source and can't work offline (that's Extract's advantage). Option B describes Extract, not Live — Live has no local snapshot at all.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: per Lesson 8, Tableau treats the result of a Custom SQL query as a single ________, which you can then use in the view exactly like any other table.
questions.explain: Custom SQL lets you hand-write a query, and Tableau treats whatever that query returns as one single table — you can drag its columns onto shelves and build views from it exactly as you would from a table you'd dragged directly onto the Data Source canvas.

questions.prompt: Match each data-preparation term to what it actually does, per Lessons 12-13.
right: One row per entity, with categories or time periods spread across separate columns
Automatically detects and cleans up messy spreadsheet layouts, like merged titles or multiple tables stacked on one sheet
Turns columns into rows, reshaping wide data into the long format Tableau generally prefers
Breaks one field into multiple fields based on a delimiter Tableau detects or you specify
questions.explain: Data Interpreter cleans up messy spreadsheet layouts automatically. Split breaks one field into several based on a delimiter. Pivot turns columns into rows, converting wide data into long. Wide data itself is the shape with categories or time periods spread across separate columns, which is exactly what Pivot fixes.

questions.prompt: What does Tableau's Show Me panel actually do when you open it, per Lesson 14?
options: It looks at the fields currently in the view or selected in the Data pane and highlights the chart types that combination can support, based on each chart type's minimum field requirements
It analyzes your data's actual values to automatically determine the single best chart for your business question
It cleans and reshapes the underlying data source before any visualization can be built
It only becomes available after you've manually built the chart type you're trying to create
It's a separate paid add-on that isn't included with a standard Tableau Desktop license
It permanently changes the data types of your fields to match whichever chart type you select
questions.explain: Show Me evaluates the fields you've already selected against each chart type's minimum requirements and lights up (or grays out) icons accordingly — it's a recommendation panel built on the same Columns/Rows/Marks mechanics you already control directly, not an analysis engine and not a separate product.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B is the tempting one because it sounds like what a 'smart suggestion' feature should do — but Lesson 14 is explicit that Show Me 'reads requirements, it doesn't read intent.' It can tell you which chart types your current fields technically support; it has no idea what business question you're actually trying to answer, so it can't determine the single 'best' chart for your purpose.

questions.prompt: A user drags Sales to Columns and Profit to Rows, with no dimension anywhere in the view. What does the resulting scatter plot show, and why?
options: A single mark — the grand total of Sales plotted against the grand total of Profit — because with no dimension present, Tableau aggregates both measures as one combined sum
One mark per row in the underlying data, since scatter plots never aggregate their measures
An error, because a scatter plot requires at least one dimension on the Marks card before it can render
A line connecting Sales and Profit over time, since both are measures
questions.explain: With two measures and no dimension, Tableau aggregates each as a sum and renders exactly one mark — the grand total of Sales against the grand total of Profit. Dragging a dimension onto Detail or Color is what splits that single mark into many, one per member of that dimension, which is the whole point of adding one.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about pie charts, donut charts, and treemaps, per Lesson 16.
options: Tableau has no built-in native donut chart type — it's built as a community workaround using a dual-axis pie
A treemap can encode two measures at once, via size and color, where a pie chart effectively only encodes one, via Angle
Pie charts remain just as readable regardless of how many categories or slices are shown
Building a donut chart requires synchronizing two pie axes so a smaller, solid circle masks the center of a larger colored one
A treemap's Angle field on the Marks card determines the size of each rectangle
questions.explain: Tableau genuinely has no native donut chart — it's a dual-axis-pie workaround. A treemap earns its advantage over a pie precisely because it can encode two measures (size and color) where a pie chart's Angle field really only encodes one. Building the donut requires Dual Axis plus Synchronize Axis so the smaller white circle masks the larger pie's center. Pie charts fall apart past a handful of slices, the opposite of option C — and a treemap has no 'Angle' field at all, since Angle is specific to pie marks; a treemap's rectangles are sized by whatever measure you drop directly, not an Angle encoding.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: per Lesson 19, when Show Me builds a histogram, it switches the Rows shelf's aggregation from SUM to ________, since a histogram plots how many rows fall into each range, not the sum of the measure itself.
questions.explain: A histogram never plots the sum of a measure — it plots how many rows fall into each bin's range. That's why Show Me swaps the Rows aggregation from SUM to Count (CNT) the moment you build a histogram, whether via Show Me or by hand.

questions.prompt: Match each analytical question to the chart-selection category it falls under, per Lesson 21's framework.
left: How has this changed over time?
Are these two measures related, and how strongly?
Which item is the biggest, and how do these compare?
What's the spread or shape of this measure?
right: Magnitude — answered by bar charts
Change over time — answered by line or area charts
Distribution — answered by histograms or box plots
Correlation — answered by scatter plots
questions.explain: 'How has this changed over time' is the Change over time category, answered with line/area charts. 'Are these two measures related' is Correlation, answered with scatter plots. 'Which item is biggest' is Magnitude, answered with bar charts. 'What's the spread or shape' is Distribution, answered with histograms or box plots — exactly Lesson 21's point that the question should pick the chart, not the other way around.

questions.prompt: On a scatter plot of Sales vs. Profit by Region, a user drags Customer Name onto Detail on the Marks card (not Color). What actually changes in the view, and why?
options: The number of marks increases to one per customer, with no new color or legend appearing, because Detail splits marks apart by a field's members without adding any visual encoding
Nothing changes, because Detail only affects tooltips, not the marks themselves
Every mark recolors by Customer Name, the same as if Customer Name had been dropped on Color instead
The view switches from a scatter plot to a bar chart, since Detail only works with discrete bar-chart views
questions.explain: Detail adds a field to the view's level of detail — marks split apart by that field's members — without adding color, size, or any other visual encoding of its own. The mark count jumps from one per Region to one per Region-Customer combination, but no legend or new color appears, which is exactly what distinguishes Detail from Color.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about titles, captions, reference lines, and annotations, per Lesson 25.
options: A worksheet's caption is auto-generated by Tableau by default, describing the fields and active filters in plain language
A reference line is tied to one specific mark, point, or area, the same as an annotation
A reference line can be computed (like an Average or Median) or set to a fixed constant value
Annotations come in three types: mark, point, and area
A title's default content is always a fixed, non-editable sheet name that can never be changed
questions.explain: Tableau auto-writes a caption describing the view's fields and filters in a plain sentence. Reference lines can be a computation (Average, Median, Total) or a fixed constant — but it's annotations, not reference lines, that tie to one specific mark/point/area; a reference line spans the whole chart for comparison. Annotations do come in exactly three types: mark, point, and area. And a title defaults to a <Sheet Name> placeholder that's fully editable via the Edit Title dialog, not a fixed, uneditable value.

questions.prompt: Put Darkhorse Analytics' chart-cleanup removal sequence, as applied in Lesson 26, in the correct order.
items: Remove backgrounds — gradients, textures, shaded plot areas
Remove redundant labels — hide a legend once its information is already shown on a header
Reduce colors — one accent color for the mark that matters, gray or neutral for the rest
Remove bolding and gridlines — anything drawn that isn't the data itself
questions.explain: The cleanup sequence from Lesson 26 (and the Darkhorse Analytics example it's drawn from) removes backgrounds first, then redundant labels/legends, then reduces color down to just what's needed, and finally strips remaining bolding and gridlines — subtraction, step by step, until only the data itself remains visually prominent.

questions.prompt: A dashboard builder wants 'the top 5 sub-categories by sales, within the Furniture category.' They build a Top 5 filter on Sub-Category by SUM(Sales) and add a Category: Furniture filter, but leave that Category filter as a regular dimension filter instead of adding it to context. What actually happens, per Lesson 30?
options: Tableau computes the Top 5 against the entire dataset first, then shows whichever of those happen to be Furniture — possibly zero, one, or all five, purely by coincidence
The result is identical either way, since filter order never changes what a Top N filter returns
Tableau raises an error, because a Top N filter can't coexist with another dimension filter on the same view
The Category filter silently overrides the Top N filter, so only Furniture's sub-categories are ever ranked regardless of context
questions.explain: Without adding Category: Furniture to context, Tableau computes the Top 5 Sub-Category filter against the whole dataset first, then the Furniture filter is applied afterward — so the result is whichever of the overall top 5 happen to be Furniture, which could be none of them. Adding the Category filter to context forces it to run first, so the Top 5 is correctly computed only among Furniture's own sub-categories.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: per Lesson 28, a ________ Date filter recalculates its window relative to today every time the workbook is opened, while a Range of Dates filter stays fixed to the exact dates you picked.
questions.explain: A Relative Date filter ('last 30 days,' 'this quarter') recalculates from today every time the view loads, which is what most live dashboards actually want. A Range of Dates filter is fixed to specific start and end dates and doesn't shift over time, better suited to a historical analysis that shouldn't change.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the Analytics pane's trend lines, forecasts, and reference lines, per Lesson 32.
options: A trend line fits a statistical model to historical data, but doesn't by itself project future values
A forecast's shaded confidence band should get narrower the further out it projects, since Tableau becomes more certain the further ahead it looks
A reference line can be a fixed constant or a computed value like Average or Median, but it doesn't fit anything to the data the way a trend line does
Right-clicking a trend line and choosing Describe Trend Model shows its actual R-squared value and statistical significance
Reference Band and Forecast are two names for the exact same Analytics pane object
questions.explain: A trend line fits a line to historical data but isn't itself a forecast — that's a separate object. A reference line marks a fixed or computed value without fitting anything. Describe Trend Model surfaces the real R-squared and significance instead of requiring you to eyeball it. A forecast's confidence band should actually widen, not narrow, the further out it projects — that's Tableau being honest that distant projections are less certain, the opposite of option B. Reference Band and Forecast are two entirely separate objects, not the same thing under different names.

questions.prompt: Put Tableau's six-stage order of operations, per Lesson 31, in the correct sequence.
questions.explain: Tableau always processes a view in this fixed order: Extract Filters, then Data Source Filters, then Context Filters (computed once, first among sheet-level filters), then Dimension Filters, then Measure Filters, and finally Table Calc Filters — which can only run last because a table calculation needs the rest of the view's data already assembled before it can compute anything.

questions.prompt: What is a calculated field in Tableau, per Lesson 33?
options: A new field you define yourself using a formula in Tableau's calculation language, built from fields that already exist in your data source
A field that only exists after a workbook has been published to Tableau Server
A physical column that gets added directly to the underlying data source the moment the formula is saved
A quick filter that recalculates automatically every time a workbook is opened
A calculation that only operates on data already aggregated into the current view
A type of field that Tableau Public specifically restricts users from creating
questions.explain: A calculated field is a field you define with your own formula — arithmetic, functions, or logic — built from fields already in the data source, and it appears in the Data pane marked with an '=' icon the moment you save it. It never touches or modifies the underlying source data itself.
questions.distractorExplain: Option E describes a table calculation, not a calculated field — and the two are genuinely easy to confuse. A calculated field (this chapter) is evaluated against the underlying data source, row by row or as an aggregate, before it ever reaches the view. A table calculation (Chapter 7) is computed afterward, on data already aggregated into the view. Mixing up which one you're building is one of the most common early Tableau mistakes.

questions.prompt: A developer writes `Profit Ratio (wrong) = [Profit] / [Sales]`, with no SUM() wrapping, then drops it on a table broken out by Category. Tableau accepts the formula and shows one number per category — but it differs from the correctly-written `SUM([Profit]) / SUM([Sales])`. Why, per Lessons 34 and 39?
options: Without explicit aggregation, Tableau computes the division row by row first and then aggregates those individual ratios, which produces a different number than dividing the two already-summed totals
Tableau actually computes the exact same number either way — the two formulas only look different because of formatting
The unwrapped formula throws a 'cannot mix aggregate and non-aggregate arguments' error and never produces a number at all
Dropping the unwrapped formula on a view silently removes Sales from the calculation entirely
questions.explain: `[Profit] / [Sales]` with no SUM() is a valid disaggregated, row-level formula — dividing each row's own Profit by its own Sales. Once placed on a view, Tableau has to aggregate that per-row result (by default, summing or averaging the individual ratios), which is a completely different number than first summing all of Profit and all of Sales and then dividing the two totals. This is exactly why Lesson 34's KPI ratio formulas wrap both sides in SUM().

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about ISNULL, IFNULL, and ZN, per Lesson 38.
options: ISNULL only tells you whether an expression is NULL — it doesn't substitute a replacement value by itself
IFNULL and ZN can both substitute a fallback value for a NULL, but ZN is specifically meant for numeric values
ZN converts any NULL value, whether numeric or text, into the number 0
Arithmetic performed directly on a NULL value in Tableau typically produces another NULL, rather than treating it as zero
IFNULL requires exactly two fallback values — one for text fields and a separate one for numeric fields
questions.explain: ISNULL is purely a yes/no test — it returns TRUE/FALSE and doesn't fix anything on its own. IFNULL substitutes a fallback for any type, while ZN is the numeric-specific shortcut equivalent to IFNULL(field, 0). Arithmetic on a NULL typically propagates NULL rather than treating it as zero, which is exactly the trap ZN and IFNULL exist to prevent. ZN specifically handles numeric NULLs, not text — using it on a text field isn't its intended job, unlike option C claims — and IFNULL takes one fallback value, not two.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: every IF block in a Tableau calculation must close with the keyword ________, or the Calculation Editor shows a syntax error before you can even save it.
questions.explain: Both IF/THEN/ELSEIF/ELSE and CASE/WHEN structures must close with END. Forgetting it is one of the most common first-time errors in Tableau's calculation language, and the Calculation Editor's status message turns red immediately if it's missing.

questions.prompt: A user puts Order Date on Columns and selects 'Month' under the Date Parts section, not Date Values. What does the resulting view actually show, and why, per Lesson 40?
options: Twelve columns, January through December, with every year's data for that month lumped together — because a Date Part ignores everything above the level you chose
One column per calendar month across every year, continuously increasing — because Date Parts stay anchored to each month's real calendar position
A single column showing only the current month
Exactly the same result as choosing Month under Date Values, since both sections behave identically
questions.explain: A Date Part bins data to a cyclical component and ignores the surrounding year — 'Month' as a Date Part lumps every May, regardless of year, into one bucket, giving you 12 columns total. Date Values, by contrast, stay anchored to the real calendar position, giving one column per actual calendar month across every year — the opposite behavior from what's described in option B.

questions.prompt: A user builds a line chart with a discrete (blue) Month field on Columns and Sales on Rows. The resulting line looks broken into disconnected segments instead of one smooth trend. What's the fix, per Lesson 41?
options: Convert the Month field from discrete to continuous, so it produces a single unbroken axis instead of separate headers
Switch the mark type from Line to Area, which automatically repairs any broken segments
Remove Sales from Rows and place it on the Marks card's Color shelf instead
Convert the Month field from a Dimension to a Measure
questions.explain: A discrete field produces separate headers with no implied continuous order, so a line chart built on one draws broken segments between each header. Converting the same field to continuous produces one unbroken axis, letting a line chart trace a single smooth trend across it — exactly the switch Lesson 41 calls the most important one for building a real time-series chart.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about table calculations, per Lessons 42 and 45.
options: A table calculation is computed on data already aggregated into the view, not on the underlying source rows
A field carrying a table calculation shows a small triangle badge on its pill
Competition ranking (1,2,2,4) matches SQL's DENSE_RANK() behavior
Dense ranking (1,2,2,3) means tied rows share a position with no skip afterward, matching SQL's DENSE_RANK()
WINDOW_AVG's two numeric arguments set which dimension the calculation partitions by
questions.explain: Table calculations recompute values from what's already aggregated into the view, and any field carrying one shows a triangle badge. Dense ranking matches SQL's DENSE_RANK() — ties share a position with no skip. Competition ranking (1,2,2,4) actually matches SQL's RANK(), not DENSE_RANK(), the reverse of option C. And WINDOW_AVG's two numeric arguments are row offsets (how far back and forward to average), not a partitioning setting — partitioning is controlled separately through Compute Using.

questions.prompt: Match each addressing/partitioning term to what it actually controls, per Lesson 46.
right: Breaks the view into separate scopes, restarting the calculation fresh inside each one
Addresses whatever's on Rows, and partitions by whatever's on Columns
Determines the direction a table calculation moves through — which cells count as before/after
Addresses whatever's on Columns, and partitions by whatever's on Rows
questions.explain: Table (Across) addresses Columns and partitions by Rows; Table (Down) is the reverse. An addressing dimension controls the direction a calculation moves through — its 'before' and 'after.' A partitioning dimension breaks the view into separate scopes, restarting the calculation inside each one — exactly like SQL's PARTITION BY and ORDER BY clauses.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes how a Tableau relationship differs from a traditional join, per Lesson 48?
options: A relationship doesn't require picking a join type up front — Tableau decides how to combine logical tables per worksheet, aggregating to the level of detail that worksheet actually needs, without duplicating rows until necessary
A relationship always produces a single flat physical table the instant two logical tables are connected
A relationship requires picking an inner, left, right, or full outer join type, exactly the same as a traditional join
A relationship can only ever be created inside the physical layer, never on the main logical-layer canvas
A relationship behaves identically to a join in every respect except its name
A relationship is only available when connecting to a published Tableau data source
questions.explain: A relationship's whole point is deferring the combine decision: no join-type picker, no immediate row duplication. Tableau waits until a specific worksheet references fields from both logical tables, then aggregates each side to exactly the level of detail that worksheet needs before combining anything — which is also why relationships avoid the fan-out problem a join can cause.
questions.distractorExplain: The most tempting wrong answer is the idea that a relationship still requires choosing an inner/left/right/full outer join type, the same way a join does — but that's backwards. The entire reason Tableau introduced relationships is to skip that up-front join-type decision and let Tableau resolve the combine automatically, per worksheet, instead.

questions.prompt: A Customers table has 100 rows (one per customer) and an Orders table has 340 rows (one per order). A developer joins Customers to Orders on CustomerID, then sums a customer-level field called Signup Bonus that lives on the Customers side. What happens to that SUM, and why, per Lesson 50?
options: It comes out too high, because each customer's Signup Bonus gets duplicated once for every order that customer placed, due to the join's row-level fan-out
It comes out exactly correct, since a join never duplicates columns that didn't originally vary
It comes out as NULL for every customer who placed more than one order
Tableau automatically detects the mismatch and divides the SUM by each customer's order count
questions.explain: Joining Customers to Orders on CustomerID duplicates each customer row once per matching order — correct for order-level questions, but wrong for a customer-level field like Signup Bonus, which gets summed once per order instead of once per customer. Every individual joined row still looks correct; only the aggregate is wrong, which is exactly what makes fan-out dangerous.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about unions and data blending, per Lessons 51-52.
options: Tableau's union behaves like SQL's UNION ALL — it keeps every row, duplicates included, rather than de-duplicating like plain UNION would
A wildcard (automatic) union only includes the tables that existed at the moment it was built — it never picks up a new matching table added later
Data blending queries each source independently, aggregates both, and stitches the aggregated results together only in the visualization itself
Blending can perform true row-level analysis across both data sources, the same way a join can
One real reason to blend instead of relate or join is that one source is a published Tableau data source, which can't be joined or related to another source
questions.explain: Tableau's union is UNION ALL behavior — every row, no de-duplication. Blending queries each source independently and only lines up the already-aggregated results visually. A published Tableau data source genuinely forces blending, since it can't be joined or related. A wildcard union does the opposite of option B — its entire purpose is automatically picking up new matching tables on future refreshes. And blending specifically cannot do row-level analysis, since every secondary-source measure is already aggregated by the time it reaches the view — the opposite of option D.

questions.prompt: Match each scenario to the right technique — relationship, join, or blend — per Lesson 53's decision process.
left: Combining Orders and Returns from the same workbook, related by Order ID
Combining a published Tableau Server data source with a local spreadsheet of quota targets
Joining Customers to Transactions where every transaction row must be intentionally duplicated per associated promo code
Needing the linking field between two sources to vary from one worksheet to another within the same workbook
right: Join — the only one of the three that intentionally duplicates rows at the row level
Blend — the only one of the three where the linking field can change per worksheet
Relationship — the default choice, no fan-out risk, covers the vast majority of day-to-day analysis
Blend — required because a published Tableau data source can't be joined or related to another source
questions.explain: Combining two tables from the same workbook on a shared key is the everyday relationship case. A published data source forces a blend, since it can't be joined or related. Intentional row-level duplication for a compliance report is exactly the case that needs a real join. And needing the linking field to vary sheet by sheet is only possible with a blend, since relationships and joins are both fixed at the data source level.

questions.prompt: Where do the Latitude and Longitude fields on a Tableau map actually come from, per Lesson 54?
options: Tableau's own internal geocoding database, matched against the text values of a field with a geographic role
Columns that must already exist in the source data before any map can be built
A calculated field the user must write manually using date functions
The Analytics pane's Model objects, like Trend Line and Forecast
questions.explain: Once a field gets a geographic role, Tableau automatically generates Latitude and Longitude measures by matching that field's text values (like 'Texas') against its own internal geocoding database — not from anything already present in the source data. That's exactly why a misspelled or unrecognized value can't be plotted: there's nothing in the database for it to match.

questions.prompt: A filled map shades each U.S. state by a raw count — total number of orders — and large states like Texas and California appear darkest. What's the likely problem with this map, per Lesson 55?
options: Large states look artificially significant simply because of their size, when a rate or per-capita value would tell a more honest story
Filled maps cannot render raw counts at all — Tableau would refuse to draw it
The map is accurate; raw counts are always the right way to compare states on a filled map
This issue only ever affects symbol maps, never filled maps
questions.explain: A filled map showing a raw count is a classic visualization trap — a bigger state looks more significant purely because it has more physical area or population, not because its rate of activity is actually higher. Filled maps should almost always show a rate or ratio, not a raw total, unless the count genuinely correlates with land area, which it almost never does.

questions.prompt: Match each mapping term to what it actually is, per Lessons 56 and 58.
right: A value matching more than one real place, forcing Tableau to guess which one is meant
A Group combining underlying regions into a business-defined boundary with no official match
A value Tableau's geocoding database has no match for at all
A join matching rows by their physical geometry relationship, like Intersects, instead of a shared key
questions.explain: An unrecognized location has no match anywhere in Tableau's geocoding database. An ambiguous location matches more than one real place, forcing a guess. A spatial join matches rows by actual geometric relationship (like Intersects) rather than a shared key. A custom territory is a Group combining real underlying regions into a business-defined boundary that doesn't correspond to any official geography.

questions.prompt: A user wants to combine 'Bookcases' and 'Tables' into one category called 'Bookcases & Tables' that shows up under that new combined name in the view. Should they build a Group or a Set, per Lessons 59-60, and why?
options: A Group, because a group relabels and combines specific members into one new named member, while a set only flags members as in/out without renaming anything
A Set, because sets are the only Tableau feature capable of combining two dimension members together
Either works identically — Group and Set are two names for the same underlying feature
Neither — this specifically requires a calculated field with a CASE statement
questions.explain: A group relabels members, combining several into one new, renamed member — exactly 'Bookcases' and 'Tables' becoming 'Bookcases & Tables.' A set does something different: it flags each member True/False for membership without renaming or combining anything, so every original member keeps its own name.

questions.prompt: A user wants a set that re-evaluates live, based on a rule spanning two different measures together — e.g., 'customers whose Sales exceed $10,000 AND whose Profit margin exceeds 20%.' They try to build this on a single dynamic set's Condition tab. What's the problem, per Lesson 60?
options: A dynamic set can only be based on a single dimension, so a rule spanning two separate conditions like this needs a calculated field or LOD expression instead
Dynamic sets can only use the Top tab, never the Condition tab, for anything besides Sales specifically
Dynamic sets cannot be created on a Customer Name field under any circumstances
A dynamic set automatically combines itself with every other set already in the workbook
questions.explain: Lesson 60 states the limitation directly: a dynamic set can only be based on a single dimension. A rule spanning two different measures together is exactly the kind of multi-condition logic that needs a calculated field (Chapter 6) or an LOD expression (Chapter 12) instead of a single set's Condition tab.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about combined sets and Set Actions, per Lesson 61.
options: 'Shared Members in Both Sets' produces the intersection — only members present in both source sets
Two sets can be combined even if they're built on two completely different dimensions, like a customer set and a product set
'Customers (2013) except shared members' isolates customers who are new in 2013 — not present in the 2012 set
A Set Action can change a set's membership live, based on a hover, select, or menu interaction on a mark
Combining two sets always produces a fixed set that can never be updated again afterward
questions.explain: Shared Members in Both Sets is the intersection. 'Customers (2013) except shared members' isolates customers unique to 2013 — genuinely new. Set Actions do update a set's membership live from a hover/select/menu interaction. Two sets being combined must be built on the same dimension — a customer set and a product set can't be combined, contrary to option B. And a combined set isn't locked forever — it can still be the target of further combination or a Set Action, contrary to option E.

questions.prompt: A user creates a parameter, shows its control, and drags the slider — the current value visibly changes, but nothing else on the worksheet reacts. What's missing, per Lesson 64?
options: No calculated field (or other object like a reference line) references the parameter yet, so nothing is wired up to respond when its value changes
Parameters never affect a view under any circumstances — they're purely cosmetic controls
The parameter's data type must be Boolean before anything can reference it
The workbook needs to be published to Tableau Server before parameters can take effect
questions.explain: A parameter is inert on its own — it's just a value sitting in the workbook. The moment a calculated field (or a reference line's Value setting) references that parameter, moving the control recalculates that field and everything built on top of it. Until that reference exists, nothing downstream has any reason to change.

questions.prompt: A team builds a dynamic measure selector using a List parameter and a CASE calculation covering four measures. Six months later, a new measure is added to the data source, and selecting it from the parameter's dropdown does nothing. Why, per Lesson 65?
options: The new measure's name was added to the parameter's list but never added as its own WHEN clause inside the CASE calculation, so the calculation has nothing to return for it
Parameters automatically expire after a fixed number of uses and must be rebuilt from scratch
A CASE calculation can only ever support exactly four WHEN clauses, with no way to add a fifth
New measures can never be referenced by any parameter, as a hard Tableau limitation
questions.explain: The selector parameter's list and the CASE calculation's WHEN clauses have to be kept in sync by hand. Adding a new measure to the parameter's list without also adding a matching WHEN clause to the CASE statement means selecting that new value returns nothing — exactly the manual-maintenance limitation Lesson 65 calls out as this technique's strain point.

questions.prompt: Match each parameter-related term to what it actually is, per Lessons 63, 66, and 67.
right: Testing how results would change under a different input, without altering the underlying data
A slider between a minimum and maximum value, with a defined step size
A fixed dropdown of specific values you define yourself
An interaction — hover, select, or menu — on a mark that sets a parameter's value automatically
questions.explain: List gives a clean dropdown of specific values you define. Range gives a slider between a min and max with a step size. A Parameter Action lets a hover, select, or menu interaction on a mark set a parameter's value directly, without the person touching its control. What-if analysis is the broader practice of testing a different input's effect without touching the actual data.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes Tableau's three LOD expression keywords, per Lesson 68?
options: FIXED computes at exactly the listed dimension(s), independent of the view; INCLUDE computes at the view's dimensions plus the listed one(s); EXCLUDE computes at the view's dimensions minus the listed one(s)
FIXED, INCLUDE, and EXCLUDE all compute identically — they're interchangeable syntax for the same operation
INCLUDE removes detail from the view, while EXCLUDE adds detail the view doesn't already have
FIXED is the only one of the three LOD keywords that responds to a regular, non-context dimension filter
EXCLUDE can only be applied to date fields, never to a dimension like Sub-Category
INCLUDE and EXCLUDE are both independent of the view, exactly the same way FIXED is
questions.explain: FIXED computes at exactly the dimensions named, ignoring the rest of the view. INCLUDE adds the listed dimension(s) on top of the view's own grain — finer detail than the view has. EXCLUDE removes the listed dimension(s) from the view's grain — coarser detail than the view has. INCLUDE and EXCLUDE are relative to the view and change if the view changes; FIXED is independent of it.
questions.distractorExplain: The most common mix-up is swapping INCLUDE and EXCLUDE's definitions outright: INCLUDE actually adds finer detail than the view has (not removes it), while EXCLUDE removes detail the view would otherwise have (not adds it). Getting the two backwards is exactly the mistake Lesson 68's side-by-side table exists to prevent.

questions.prompt: A `{ FIXED [Customer Name] : SUM([Sales]) }` calculation sits on a view, and a regular (non-context) dimension filter sets Region to West. A customer has orders in both East and West. What happens to that customer's FIXED value, per Lesson 69?
options: It keeps showing that customer's total sales across every region, unchanged, because a regular dimension filter runs after FIXED has already computed
It immediately shrinks to just that customer's West-region sales, since every filter applies before any calculation runs
It returns NULL, because FIXED can't be combined with any filter at all
It throws a 'cannot mix aggregate and non-aggregate arguments' error
questions.explain: FIXED computes before ordinary dimension filters are applied in Tableau's order of operations, so a regular Region filter doesn't change its result — the customer's full East-plus-West total keeps showing. Only promoting that filter to a context filter (which runs before FIXED) would make the FIXED calculation reflect just West.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about LOD expressions vs. table calculations, per Lesson 72.
options: A table calculation can reference a dimension that isn't anywhere on the current view, the same way an LOD expression can
A table calculation's result can change if you simply change the sort order or layout of the view, even with the same underlying data
An LOD expression computes at query time, as part of the request sent to the data source, before the view's own aggregation happens
Running totals, rank, and moving averages are all things an LOD expression can do just as naturally as a table calculation
If a calculation's definition depends on row order or table layout, it must be a table calculation, never an LOD expression
questions.explain: Table calculations are genuinely sensitive to the view's layout and sort order, since they operate on position within the visible table. LOD expressions compute at query time, against the underlying data source, before the view's aggregation happens. And anything position-dependent — running totals, rank, moving averages — structurally has to be a table calculation, since LOD expressions have no concept of 'the row above this one.' A table calculation can't reach a dimension that isn't already part of the view's result set, the opposite of option A, and that position-dependence is exactly why an LOD expression can't replicate running totals or rank, contrary to option D.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: per Lesson 73, a FIXED LOD expression can compute something that isn't even present anywhere on the current ________, which is exactly what lets `{ FIXED [Customer Name] : SUM([Sales]) }` work correctly even when Customer Name itself isn't dragged onto the view at all.
questions.explain: Because FIXED computes against the underlying data source at query time rather than against whatever's already on the view, it can use a dimension — like Customer Name — that never appears on Rows, Columns, or the Marks card at all. A table calculation has no equivalent reach, since it only works with dimensions already part of the view's result set.

questions.prompt: A developer builds a dual-axis chart combining Sales and Profit Ratio — two measures on very different scales — then right-clicks and chooses Synchronize Axis, forcing both onto the same numeric scale. What's the likely result, per Lesson 74?
options: One of the two lines becomes visually flattened or unreadable, since synchronizing forces two genuinely different-scale measures to share a single scale meant for neither of them
Synchronize Axis has no visible effect unless the two axes also share the same mark type
The chart automatically reverts back to a single-axis view
Synchronizing always improves readability, regardless of the two measures' underlying scales
questions.explain: Synchronize Axis is meant for two measures that share the same unit and genuinely benefit from a direct visual comparison. Forcing it onto a pair like Sales (tens of thousands) and Profit Ratio (a small percentage) squashes the smaller-scale measure's line nearly flat, since both now have to fit the same scale built for Sales' much larger range.

questions.prompt: A Pareto chart's rising cumulative-percentage line is built from which combination of Tableau features, per Lesson 76?
options: A dual axis on a second Sales pill, with Running Total and Percent of Total table calculations applied to it
A single LOD expression using the FIXED keyword
A dedicated 'Pareto' mark type selected directly from Show Me
A Forecast object dragged from the Analytics pane
questions.explain: A Pareto chart isn't a separate Tableau feature — it's Lesson 74's dual-axis technique combined with Chapter 7's table calculations: a second Sales pill on the same axis, with Running Total and Percent of Total applied so it renders as a rising cumulative-percentage line over the sorted bars.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: Tableau has no native Show Me chart type for either a waterfall or a funnel chart — a waterfall is built as a technique using the ________ mark type plus a running total for each segment's starting position, per Lesson 76.
questions.explain: A waterfall chart uses Gantt bars, where the bar's length is a (possibly negative) measure and its starting position comes from a running-total table calculation. A funnel chart is a separate technique — centered bars with a calculated padding measure — but also has no dedicated Show Me option.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes the difference between a tiled and a floating dashboard object, per Lesson 80?
options: A tiled object lives in an automatically-adjusting grid, resizing alongside its neighbors; a floating object sits at a fixed position and size, ignoring the grid entirely
A floating object is Tableau's default layout mode for every new object added to a dashboard
A tiled object can only ever be a worksheet — never a filter, legend, or other object
Floating objects automatically resize their neighbors whenever they're moved
Tiled and floating are two different names for the exact same layout behavior
A floating object can only ever be added inside a Horizontal layout container
questions.explain: Tiled objects live in a grid that reflows as you add, move, or resize pieces. Floating objects sit at an exact position and size on top of that grid, and moving one doesn't affect anything else on the dashboard.
questions.distractorExplain: The most tempting wrong answer is that floating is Tableau's default — it's actually the reverse: tiled is the default mode for every new object you add, and you have to deliberately flip the Tiled/Floating switch in the Objects panel before dragging something in for it to float.

questions.prompt: A developer sets a filter action to trigger on Hover over a dense scatter plot with hundreds of marks. What problem does this likely cause, per Lesson 82?
options: Every stray mouse movement re-filters the whole dashboard, which reads as broken rather than genuinely interactive
Hover-triggered filter actions are automatically disabled by Tableau on any scatter plot
Nothing changes — Hover and Select behave identically for a filter action
The filter action silently converts itself into a highlight action instead
questions.explain: Hover fires the instant the pointer rests on a mark, which is exactly why Lesson 82 flags it as a common mistake for filter actions on a dense view — every incidental mouse movement re-filters the dashboard. Select is the safer trigger for anything that actually removes data from view; Hover works better for highlight actions, where rapid dimming/un-dimming feels natural.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about Tableau's six dashboard action types, per Lesson 83.
options: A URL action is the one action type that can reach outside the Tableau workbook entirely, to an external web address
A Set Action defines only one behavior — what happens when the action runs — unlike every other action type
A Parameter Action lets a click or hover on a mark set a parameter's value, instead of requiring a viewer to use its control
All six action types — Filter, Highlight, Go to URL, Go to Sheet, Change Parameter, and Change Set Values — are added from the same Actions dialog
A Go to Sheet action removes data from the target sheet, the same way a filter action does
questions.explain: A URL action genuinely reaches outside the workbook to a web address. A Parameter Action lets a mark interaction set a parameter directly. All six action types share the same Actions dialog's Add Action dropdown. A Set Action actually defines two behaviors, not one — what happens when the action runs and what happens when the selection clears — which is what makes it different from the others, the opposite of option B. A Go to Sheet action navigates the viewer to a different sheet; it doesn't filter or remove any data, unlike a filter action, contrary to option E.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 79's recommended 5-step dashboard build order, when should the KPI header and any global filters be added to a dashboard?
options: Last, once the rest of the dashboard's actual shape is visible, so the header's width and placement make sense against it
First, before any other worksheet is placed on the canvas
It doesn't matter — build order has no effect on the final layout
Immediately after setting the dashboard's size, before any worksheet is even finished
questions.explain: Lesson 79's build order finishes every worksheet first, sets the dashboard size, places the largest/most important view as an anchor, adds supporting views and filters, and only then adds the KPI header and global filters last — once the dashboard's actual shape is visible enough for the header's width and placement to make sense.

questions.prompt: Match each desktop dashboard pattern to its recommended phone-layout equivalent, per Lesson 85.
left: Dense scatter plot with many marks
right: Simplify, or move to a secondary/detail screen reached by navigation
Switch to Select, since there's no hover on a touchscreen
Cut to essential columns, or replace with a summary chart
Stack vertically, or keep only the 1-2 most critical KPIs
questions.explain: A desktop KPI row stacks vertically (or trims to the most critical KPIs) on phone. Hover-triggered actions have to switch to Select, since touchscreens have no hover. A wide detail table gets cut to essential columns or replaced with a summary. A dense scatter plot gets simplified or pushed to a secondary screen — phone design is a different information hierarchy, not a shrunken desktop layout.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: per Lesson 86, switching a published data source from a live connection to an ________ is one of the most common fixes for a dashboard that feels slow, since the dashboard then queries a local, optimized copy instead of re-running a slow source query on every filter change.
questions.explain: A live connection re-runs its query against the source every time a filter changes, which is slow if that source is itself slow or remote. Switching to an extract means the dashboard queries a local, Hyper-optimized copy instead — one of several performance fixes Lesson 86 traces directly back to a decision made in an earlier chapter (Chapter 2's Live vs. Extract choice).

questions.prompt: A company wants Tableau's full server feature set but has strict compliance rules requiring their data to stay on infrastructure they fully control. Which product should they choose, and why, per Lesson 87?
options: Tableau Server, because it's the identical product to Tableau Cloud feature-for-feature, but self-hosted by the company's own organization instead of by Tableau
Tableau Public, because it's free and therefore has no data-residency implications
Tableau Desktop, because it never connects to any server at all
Tableau Cloud, because Tableau's own infrastructure is automatically compliant with every possible regulation
questions.explain: Tableau Server and Tableau Cloud share the identical publishing, permission, and sharing feature set — the one structural difference is who hosts it. A company with strict compliance or data-residency requirements chooses Server specifically because the data never leaves infrastructure the company itself controls, unlike Cloud, which Tableau hosts and operates.

questions.prompt: An executive wants to be notified the instant profit drops below a specific target, rather than waiting for a scheduled weekly email. Which Tableau feature fits that need, per Lesson 89?
options: A data-driven alert, since it's condition-based and notifies the moment a value crosses a defined threshold
A subscription, since it's condition-based and fires immediately whenever any underlying data changes
A permission rule, since it controls who is allowed to see a view at all
A refresh schedule, since it determines how often a published extract updates
questions.explain: A data-driven alert watches a continuous numeric axis and fires the moment a value crosses a defined threshold — exactly 'the instant profit drops below target.' A subscription is schedule-based, not condition-based — it sends a snapshot on a fixed calendar (like every Monday), regardless of whether anything crossed a threshold in between.

questions.prompt: A developer wants to find the single biggest bottleneck in a slow workbook, without hunting through a chronological record of everything that happened. Which Performance Recording view should they check, per Lesson 90?
options: The Events view, since it sorts every recorded event by duration, longest first
The Timeline view, since it only lays out events in the order they occurred, not by duration
The Query view, since it always lists the single slowest event at the top regardless of its actual duration
The Extract History dialog, since it automatically records every performance event
questions.explain: The Events view takes the same recorded events as the Timeline and sorts them by duration, longest first — exactly the view for finding the actual bottleneck without hunting. The Timeline view is for seeing when things happened relative to each other (a one-time cost vs. a recurring one), and the Query view shows the literal query text for query events specifically, not a ranked list of every event type.

questions.prompt: Project 1's Executive Sales Dashboard colors its U.S. map by Profit Ratio instead of raw Sales. Per Lesson 92, why is that the stronger design choice?
options: Profit Ratio shows where the business is actually healthy, not just where it happens to be big, which is a more useful story for a map's color encoding
Raw Sales cannot be mapped at all, since it isn't a geographic field
Profit Ratio is required because Tableau's default map color is always a ratio measure
There's no real difference — either measure tells the exact same story once placed on a map
questions.explain: Lesson 92 is explicit that Profit Ratio is more interesting on the map than raw Sales, because it reveals where the business is genuinely healthy rather than simply where it's large — a region can have huge Sales and still be a weak performer once profitability is considered.

questions.prompt: Project 2's Customer Segmentation Dashboard builds Recency, Frequency, and Monetary as three separate FIXED LOD expressions. Per Lesson 93, what's the single most important verification step before trusting the segmentation built on top of them?
options: Manually check the Recency, Frequency, and Monetary values against two or three individual customers by hand in the underlying data, since a wrong FIXED dimension makes every downstream segment wrong too
Confirm the three fields are written as table calculations rather than LOD expressions
Verify the scatter plot renders using exactly the same color palette as the KPI header
Make sure the segmentation calculated field uses SUM instead of COUNTD for every metric
questions.explain: Lesson 93 calls the FIXED LOD expressions 'unforgiving' — get the fixed dimension wrong and every downstream segment inherits that error. Spot-checking the three RFM fields against a couple of real customers by hand is the concrete way to catch that before building the rest of the dashboard on top of a wrong foundation.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: per Lesson 95, an interview question that tests whether you've actually operated a specific feature — like walking through publishing a workbook, or showing a FIXED LOD expression you personally wrote — is called a ________ question, as opposed to a conceptual one.
questions.explain: Lesson 95 splits Tableau interview questions into two categories: conceptual questions test whether you understand a tradeoff in the abstract, while tool-specific questions test whether you've actually operated the feature — which is exactly why pointing to a real project from Chapter 17 answers a tool-specific question far better than describing the feature in general terms.
